bib.title: VizWiz Grand Challenge: Answering Visual Questions from Blind People

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "VizWiz Grand Challenge: Answering Visual Questions from Blind People", Gurari, Li, Stangl, Guo, Lin, Grauman, Luo, Bigham. CVPR 2018 (the copy read is arXiv 1802.08218v4, 9 May 2018).

COVERAGE: All 16 pages, 57,654 of 57,654 chars: the main paper, the references (skimmed) and the supplementary material on pp. 11–16, which holds Tables 5 and 6.

CLAIMS
1. Dataset size and how it was collected
- number: 31,173 visual questions with 10 answers each, filtered down from 48,169 shareable ones (72,205 asked in total by 11,045 users). The split is 20,000 train / 3,173 val / 8,000 test.
- setup: Blind users of the VizWiz app took a phone photo and recorded a spoken question. Questions were transcribed on Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). About 31% were filtered out for PII, location, indecent content, "suspicious" complex scenes or low-quality images, plus 7,477 with a missing question. Answers came from US AMT workers following the VQA 1.0 protocol.
- quote: "VizWiz consists of over 31,000 visual questions originating from blind people who each took a picture using a mobile phone and recorded a spoken question" (p1); "In total, ∼31% of visual questions (i.e., 14,796) were filtered from the original 48,169" (p5)

2. Share of questions that cannot be answered
- number: 28.63%
- setup: A question counts as unanswerable when at least half of its 10 answers are "unanswerable" or "unsuitable image". "Unsuitable Image" was defined as "all white, all black, or too blurry".
- quote: "We find 28.63% of visual questions are not answerable." (p6). Causes: "blur, inadequate lighting, finger covering the lens, etc." (p2)

3. Image quality
- number: 28% of images
- setup: An image is counted when at least 2 of its 10 workers answered "unsuitable image". This is the only statistic on image quality. There is no blur metric or per-cause breakdown.
- quote: "We found 28% of images were labelled as such." (p6)
- note: Table 4 says unanswerable makes up 34.6% of answer types, which does not match the 28.63% above. The paper does not explain the difference.

4. Models trained on VQA v2 versus fine-tuned
- number: about 0.14 accuracy off the shelf. Fine-tuned models reach 0.466–0.475. Models trained only on VizWiz reach 0.465–0.469. Humans reach 0.75.
- setup: Test set of 8,000. The three models are Goyal et al. [18] (Q+I), attention [24] (Q+I+A) and bottom-up/top-down attention [6] (Q+I+BUA). Each predicts its top 3,000 answers and is scored with VQA accuracy. The cause offered is answer-vocabulary mismatch: "only 824 out of the top 3,000 answers in VizWiz are included" in VQA 2.0. Off-the-shelf accuracy on unanswerable questions is 0.060–0.071, against 0.770–0.805 after adaptation (Table 4).
- quote: "these models perform poorly, as indicated by low values for all metrics; e.g., ∼0.14 accuracy for all algorithms" (p7); "We find little performance difference between fine-tuning and training from scratch" (p7)

5. The domain shift runs both ways
- number: 0.218 to 0.318
- setup: The six models trained or fine-tuned on VizWiz were tested on the VQA 2.0 test set (Table 5, p14).
- quote: "do not generalize well; i.e., accuracy scores range from 0.218 to 0.318" (p8)

6. Predicting whether a question is answerable
- number: average precision (AP) 0.306 for the existing relevance model, 0.640 from image features alone, 0.717 for question plus image (F1 0.648)
- setup: The baseline is Mahendru et al. [30], a caption-question similarity model trained on QRPE. The new models are LSTM encoders and ResNet-152 pool5 features feeding a softmax, trained for 10 epochs (Table 6, p14).
- quote: "AP score of 30.6 for [30] versus 71.7 for Q+I" (p8); "the image provides the greatest predictive power (i.e., AP = 64)" (p8)

LIMITS
- The paper never measures image quality directly. There are no blur, lighting or framing counts, and no split between unsuitable-image and unanswerable reasons, even though it collected both labels.
- The filtering removed suspicious low-quality images (578) and complex scenes (725), so the released set probably understates how bad the raw images were. The authors raise this concern themselves.
- It does not separate the effect of image quality from the effect of answer vocabulary. The off-the-shelf failure is blamed mainly on the 824/3,000 answer overlap, not on photo quality. So it does not show that clean-photo training alone causes the drop.
- All models are 2017-era classifiers over a fixed answer set. There are no generative vision-language models (VLMs), so the absolute numbers are dated.
- Human agreement is measured by exact string match, which the authors call a lower bound.
- The 28.63% and 34.6% unanswerable figures are not reconciled.

BUILDS ON
- Bigham et al. 2010, "VizWiz: Nearly real-time answers to visual questions", UIST (the app and the data source)
- Brady et al., CHI, "Visual challenges in the everyday lives of blind people" (year cut off in the extraction)
- Antol et al. 2015, VQA, ICCV (answer protocol and accuracy metric)
- Goyal et al. 2016, "Making the V in VQA matter", arXiv
- Anderson et al. 2017, bottom-up/top-down attention, arXiv
- Mahendru et al. [30], the QRPE relevance model (its reference entry was not read in full)

CODE: none.

FIGURES
- Fig. 1, p2: "Examples of visual questions asked by blind people and corresponding answers agreed upon by crowd workers. The examples include questions that both can be answered from the image (top row) and cannot be answered from the image (bottom row)." This is the best candidate for the clean-screenshot versus phone-photo pitfall. It shows blur, framing and finger-on-lens failures in one glance.
- Fig. 5, p8 (precision-recall curves for answerability) is a second option.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction is clean. There are no embedded instructions.
- In Section 5.1 the labels look swapped: "Q+I [24], Q+I+A [18]". Tables 3 and 4 give Q+I [18] and Q+I+A [24].
- The text says the attention models "consistently outperform", but in Table 3 Q+I+BUA [6] scores 0.134, below Q+I at 0.137.
- The text says the filtering removed "∼31% (i.e., 14,796)" of 48,169, but 48,169 − 31,173 = 16,996. That arithmetic is mine, not the paper's.
